# LlamaIndex
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/start/quickstarts/llamaindex

Install, instrument, and see your first trace.

Three steps to your first LlamaIndex trace. For workflow steps, retrieval, the reaper, and options, see [the full guide](/start/integrations/llamaindex).

## Install

```bash theme={null}
pip install 'failproofai-sdk[llamaindex]'
```

## Instrument

LlamaIndex's agent API is async. Every scope works under `async with` as well as `with`.

```python theme={null}
import asyncio

import failproofai_sdk

failproofai_sdk.configure(environment="production")
failproofai_sdk.instrument()


async def main():
    async with failproofai_sdk.session():
        await agent.run("...")


asyncio.run(main())
```

> [!WARNING]
>
> Without one extra argument on your LLM, every token count in your trace is null — `llama-index-llms-openai` does not request usage when it streams. See [Token counts](/start/integrations/llamaindex#token-counts).

## Check it arrived

Run it once, then open **Observe → Sessions** and select your environment. Your run appears as a reconstructed trace.

If nothing arrives, confirm the machine is connected with `failproofai config --status`.

> **[Full LlamaIndex guide](/start/integrations/llamaindex)**
>
> Token counts, what gets recorded, workflow steps, retrieval, options, and common problems.


# Pydantic AI
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/start/quickstarts/pydantic-ai

Install, instrument, and see your first trace.

Three steps to your first Pydantic AI trace. For tools, retries, streaming, and options, see [the full guide](/start/integrations/pydantic-ai).

## Install

```bash theme={null}
pip install 'failproofai-sdk[pydantic-ai]'
```

## Instrument

```python theme={null}
import failproofai_sdk
from pydantic_ai import Agent

failproofai_sdk.configure(environment="production")
failproofai_sdk.instrument()          # before constructing any Agent

agent = Agent("openai:gpt-4o-mini", system_prompt="Be terse.")

with failproofai_sdk.session():
    result = agent.run_sync("...")
```

> [!WARNING]
>
> `instrument()` must run **before** you construct an `Agent`. The capability is appended at construction, so an agent built earlier records nothing — with no error, because nothing went wrong. This is the most common cause of an empty trace with this adapter, and module-scope agents are where it bites: import `failproofai_sdk` and call `instrument()` before importing the module that builds them.

## Check it arrived

Run it once, then open **Observe → Sessions** and select your environment. Your run appears as a reconstructed trace.

If nothing arrives, confirm the machine is connected with `failproofai config --status`.

> **[Full Pydantic AI guide](/start/integrations/pydantic-ai)**
>
> What gets recorded, tools and retries, streaming, span naming, options, and common problems.


# Choose your setup
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/start/setup

Choose local enforcement, Failproof AI Cloud, or an enterprise deployment.

> **Local enforcement**
>
> Set a machine up with no Cloud key and take a policy pack. Use this when you need immediate guardrails without sending session data to Cloud.

> **Failproof AI Cloud**
>
> Add centralized sessions, audits, online evaluations, dashboards, alerts, and fleet policy deployment.

> **Enterprise deployment**
>
> Use organization controls, scoped keys, private infrastructure, and deployment-specific security requirements.

## Enforce locally

Run `failproofai config` without a key, then take a pack with `failproofai policies add FailproofAI/policies`. In a terminal, pick **Not now — stay local** when setup asks to connect to Cloud; with no terminal and no `FAILPROOFAI_CLOUD_TOKEN`, it stays local on its own. The daemon and hooks enforce on the machine, and no session data is sent to Cloud. To connect later, follow the steps below.

## Recommended production path

1. Connect a non-production machine with transcript capture enabled.
2. Verify sessions and evaluations in Cloud.
3. Create an audit for a known failure mode.
4. Deploy the first policy in observe mode.
5. Expand to production after reviewing matches and false positives.

## Connect a machine to Cloud

**Dashboard**

1. Go to **Administration → Keys** and create a key with `events:add` and `policies:pull`.
2. Copy the one-time secret to the target machine.
3. After running the CLI connection command, go to **Admin → enforcement** and confirm the machine appears.
4. Go to **Observe → Events** and confirm its first event arrives.

The key drawer shows the two grants needed by a connected machine: event ingestion and policy delivery.

![The new API key drawer used to grant event ingestion and policy delivery permissions.](https://mintcdn.com/exosphere/WgPwQzedeDNwJBTy/images/dashboard/key-create.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=WgPwQzedeDNwJBTy\&q=85\&s=a428bdae79f837471acb66414ff6455b)

After connection, the machine should appear in enforcement with its desired and reported policy state.

![The Enforcement fleet with an enrolled machine expanded to show its desired policy state and deployment status.](https://mintcdn.com/exosphere/WgPwQzedeDNwJBTy/images/dashboard/enforcement-fleet.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=WgPwQzedeDNwJBTy\&q=85\&s=96be13256ef7e3fa89eeefcc4f1b7f10)

The first arriving event confirms that the daemon can deliver data to Cloud, independently of policy deployment.

![The live event stream showing recent agent, model, and tool events.](https://mintcdn.com/exosphere/WgPwQzedeDNwJBTy/images/dashboard/events-stream-current.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=WgPwQzedeDNwJBTy\&q=85\&s=e87ba86b877f602de73237d5a3565269)

Continue only after both the machine and its first event are visible.

**CLI**

Read the one-time secret into the shell. `read -s` takes it at a prompt that does not echo, so it never appears in a command or in shell history:

```bash theme={null}
read -rs FAILPROOFAI_CLOUD_TOKEN && export FAILPROOFAI_CLOUD_TOKEN
```

Then set the machine up, choose its policies, and name it:

```bash theme={null}
failproofai config

failproofai policies add FailproofAI/policies
failproofai config --machine-label checkout-runner-01
failproofai config --status
```

`failproofai config` does the whole setup — daemon, hooks for every agent CLI it finds, and the Cloud connection — then chooses no policies, which is what the second command is for.

The label comes **after** connecting, not during: `failproofai config --machine-label <name>` renames a machine that is already connected, and on one that is not it does nothing but say so.

Add `--no-transcripts` when transcript content must remain local.

In CI, set `FAILPROOFAI_CLOUD_TOKEN` from the secret store instead of `read -s`, and keep shell tracing (`set -x`) off, or the trace prints the key.

> [!WARNING]
>
> On a machine that is **already** set up, `failproofai config --connect <url>` enrols it and nothing else. Do not use that form for a first install: it returns before the daemon or any hook is in place, leaving a machine that shows up in Cloud but collects and enforces nothing.

Connecting to Cloud verifies event ingestion and policy delivery independently. A key may therefore be valid but missing one required permission. Use `failproofai config --status` to see which capability is configured.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Cloud setup writes local credentials only after the relevant capability succeeds. A failed verification does not leave a machine looking connected when it is not.


# Use Jev
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/start/use-jev

Set up Jev evaluations for finished sessions or Jev policies for live tool-call review.

Jev helps at two points in an agent run: score a finished session against known answers, or review a tool call in the context of what you asked the agent to do.

**Jev evals**

Use a Jev eval when a finished session can be scored against a question with a few known answers, such as “Did the customer ask for a refund? Answer yes or no.” It helps you find patterns across sessions.

## Create an eval

In the Cloud dashboard, open **Analyze → eval authoring → new eval**. Enter one fixed-answer question, select **draft**, and check that it chose a classifier score. [Test it](/evaluations/test) on real sessions, then deploy it.

![The shared eval authoring form where you describe a question, review the draft, and deploy it. This screenshot shows a code draft; use a fixed-answer question for Jev.](https://mintcdn.com/exosphere/k_s8fY_jSxA_m1d_/images/dashboard/eval-authoring-draft.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=k_s8fY_jSxA_m1d_\&q=85\&s=7738fc3dd02d1e9b1792ce401a400149)

## Read the scores

After a new session completes, open **Observe → Evaluations** or use the Cloud CLI:

```bash theme={null}
fp evals --since 7d
fp evals --aggregate --since 7d
```

The CLI reads scores; creating a Jev eval currently uses the dashboard. See [Jev evaluations](/evaluations/jev) for question types and examples.

**Jev policies**

Use Jev policy review when a string-matching policy needs the context of your request to decide whether a tool call is safe. Start in **observe** mode so you can inspect Jev's answers while your installed policies still decide each call.

Jev's checks come from a pack; Failproof AI ships none. Until you install them, Jev asks nothing, even when it is configured:

```bash theme={null}
failproofai policies add FailproofAI/jev-policies
```

## Set up Cloud Jev

In the Cloud dashboard, open **Administration → Keys** and create a key with the **machine** preset. Use it with `failproofai config` as shown in the [quickstart](/start/quickstart). On a machine without an existing Jev configuration, this enables Cloud Jev in observe mode. Check the connection with:

```bash theme={null}
failproofai jev status
failproofai jev test
```

## Use your own endpoint

In the local dashboard, open **Settings → Jev**. Choose the provider, paste its token, select **observe**, and turn Jev on.

![The local Jev settings panel with a provider, token field, and observe mode selected.](https://mintcdn.com/exosphere/iOjAK1F5HjkAlttv/images/dashboard/jev-settings.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=iOjAK1F5HjkAlttv\&q=85\&s=cdfbae016b662739a213d9507fdfbd43)

Or configure and test your endpoint from a terminal:

```bash theme={null}
failproofai jev --url https://api.typesafe.ai/v1 --mode observe --key-stdin < ~/typesafe.key
failproofai jev test
```

Ask a hooked agent to use its file-reading tool on `README.md`. Confirm that tool call appears in the session, then inspect it under **Policies → Activity** in the local dashboard. Once the observe results look right, [Jev policies](/policies/jev) explains when to enforce. For provider details and configuration, see the [integration reference](/reference/jev).


# Create a recurring audit.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/create-a-recurring-audit

/reference/openapi.json post /audits
An audit sweeps a window of your events on a schedule and files findings for
the failure patterns it sees. `schedule_interval_secs` must be between 3600
(1h) and 604800 (7d) and defaults to daily; `lookback_window_secs` must be
between 3600 (1h) and 7776000 (90d) and defaults to 7d. `schedule_anchor`
fixes the phase — runs land on `anchor + N * interval` — and defaults to the
next 09:00 UTC; an anchor more than 365 days out is rejected. The first run
is queued immediately on create regardless of the anchor.



# Delete an audit.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/delete-an-audit

/reference/openapi.json delete /audits/{id}
Cascades: the audit's queue row, its run history and all of its findings go
with it, and this cannot be undone. Muting feedback survives — it is keyed on
the fingerprint, not the audit. Requires `audits:write`; there is no separate
delete permission.



# Delete auditscontracts
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/delete-auditscontracts

/reference/openapi.json delete /audits/contracts/{cid}
Delete a contract. The agent is audited from then on as though one had never been written. Audits that already ran keep their record of what they graded against.



# Fetch one audit definition.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/fetch-one-audit-definition

/reference/openapi.json get /audits/{id}
Same shape as an entry in the list, read straight from the database rather
than the 60-second list cache — schedule state and the last-run summary are
current as of the request.



# Fetch one finding in full.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/fetch-one-finding-in-full

/reference/openapi.json get /audits/findings/{fid}
The same shape the list returns — evidence, priority factors,
recommendation, suggested alert, and the issue it graduated into.



# Get audits context
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/get-audits-context

/reference/openapi.json get /audits/{id}/context
Read an audit's extra context: the operator's written brief, plus the reference URLs it draws on and the state of each one's stored snapshot. Snapshot text is returned as a bounded preview rather than in full.



# Get auditscontracts
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/get-auditscontracts

/reference/openapi.json get /audits/contracts
List this organization's agent contracts. A contract states what one agent is for — what it must produce, how often it should run, what it must never do — and audits grade that agent against it. Contracts are organization-wide: there is one per agent, shared by every audit that covers it. Contract text is omitted here; read a single contract to get it. `last_matched` is when that agent last produced anything an audit could grade, and a contract that has never matched usually names an agent that does not exist.



# Get auditscontracts 1
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/get-auditscontracts-1

/reference/openapi.json get /audits/contracts/{cid}
Read one agent contract, including its full text. `sections` lists the parts of the document that were recognised, so a heading that was not understood is visible rather than silently having no effect.



# List an audit's runs, newest first.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/list-an-audits-runs-newest-first

/reference/openapi.json get /audits/{id}/runs
Each run carries its status, the window it covered, its finding counts and
the LLM report when there is one. An unknown audit id — or one in another
organization — returns an empty list rather than 404.



# List findings across every audit in the organization, highest priority
first.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/list-findings-across-every-audit-in-the-organization-highest-priorityfirst

/reference/openapi.json get /audits/findings
This is the triage queue. Without a `status` filter it shows only the live
set — `open` and `recurring` — so triaged findings disappear from it; pass
`status` explicitly to see them. Narrow to one audit with `audit_id`, or to
the findings one run produced or touched with `run_id`. Each finding's
`issue_id` is the issue it graduated into, or null if it never did.



# List this organization's audits, newest first.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/list-this-organizations-audits-newest-first

/reference/openapi.json get /audits
Each entry is the full definition plus its schedule state
(`next_attempt_at`, `last_attempted_at`, `last_error`), its open finding
count, and the status of its most recent run. Edits made through this API
show up immediately, but the response is cached for 60 seconds, so schedule
state advanced by the dispatcher can lag by that much.



# Post audits contextrefresh
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/post-audits-contextrefresh

/reference/openapi.json post /audits/{id}/context/refresh
Queue a re-fetch of this audit's reference URLs. Returns as soon as the work is queued, not when it finishes. Sources whose URL was refused are left alone, since nothing about them can change until the URL is edited, and a source that already has usable text keeps serving it while the re-fetch runs.



# Post auditscontracts
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/post-auditscontracts

/reference/openapi.json post /audits/contracts
Write a contract for one agent. `agent_id` must match the agent id in your telemetry exactly — take it from the agent list rather than typing it, because a name that matches nothing is not rejected and the contract simply never applies. Case and surrounding whitespace are ignored when matching. One contract per agent: writing a second for the same agent is a conflict, not a replacement. The body is Markdown and is stored as written; the response reports which sections were recognised.



# Put audits context
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/put-audits-context

/reference/openapi.json put /audits/{id}/context
Replace an audit's extra context. This is a full replacement, not a merge: the brief and the reference URL list are both set to exactly what you send, so send an empty value to clear one. Context is edited here rather than through the audit itself, so an ordinary unrelated edit to the audit can never overwrite it.



# Put auditscontracts
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/put-auditscontracts

/reference/openapi.json put /audits/contracts/{cid}
Replace a contract. This is a full replacement, not a merge: the agent id and body are set to exactly what you send. Editing a contract changes what future audits expect; findings already raised keep referring to the text that was in force when they were raised.



# Run an audit now.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/run-an-audit-now

/reference/openapi.json post /audits/{id}/run
Makes the audit's queue row due immediately; the dispatcher claims it on its
next tick, so the 202 means "queued", not "finished" — poll
`GET /audits/{id}/runs` for the result. Three cases all answer 409 and are
distinguished by the `error` field: the audit is unknown or belongs to
another organization, it is disabled (a disabled audit has no queue row), or
a run is already in progress, which must finish before another can be queued.



# Triage a finding.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/triage-a-finding

/reference/openapi.json post /audits/findings/{fid}/status
`action` is one of `ack`, `mute`, `dismiss`, `resolve`, `reopen` or
`assign`; `assign` additionally requires `assigned_to`, and any action may
carry a free-text `reason`.

`mute` and `dismiss` record durable feedback keyed on the finding's
fingerprint, which suppresses that pattern across EVERY audit in the
organization — not just the one you are looking at. `reopen` clears that
suppression. `resolve` records none, so a pattern that comes back is filed
again as new. `ack` keeps the finding visible but deprioritized.

Set `X-AgentEye-Actor` to attribute the action to a person; without it the
API key's id is recorded instead. If the finding graduated into an issue,
the issue is updated to match on a best-effort basis — a failure there is
logged and does not fail the triage, which has already committed.



# Update an audit definition.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/audits/update-an-audit-definition

/reference/openapi.json put /audits/{id}
`name` is required and always overwritten; every other field is optional and
an omitted one keeps its current value — there is no way to clear a field
back to NULL here. The same ranges as create apply. A changed
`schedule_interval_secs` or `schedule_anchor` takes effect at the next
reschedule, not on the run already queued.



# Get authintrospect
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/auth/get-authintrospect

/reference/openapi.json get /auth/introspect
Describe the API key making this request: the organization it belongs to and the permissions it holds. Requires no permission of its own — any valid key may describe itself, and only itself. Intended to be called once when provisioning a machine, so a bad key, a missing permission and a wrong organization can be told apart before anything is sent. A key that has just been revoked or has just expired may still be reported as valid for up to a minute.



# Add a tile to a dashboard.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/dashboards/add-a-tile-to-a-dashboard

/reference/openapi.json post /dashboards/{id}/tiles
A tile renders exactly one saved query: `query_id` names it, `chart_type`
is one of `line`, `area`, `bar`, `stacked_bar`, `pie`, `kpi` or `table`, and
`pos_x` / `pos_y` / `pos_w` / `pos_h` place it on the grid (origin
top-left, width and height in grid cells). `chart_config` and
`param_bindings` are opaque JSON objects the dashboard UI owns; both
default to `{}`.

The saved query must be one of your organization's — a `query_id` from
anywhere else reads as "does not exist".



# Create a dashboard.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/dashboards/create-a-dashboard

/reference/openapi.json post /dashboards
`definition` is an opaque JSON object owned by the dashboard UI (filters and
display settings) — it is stored and returned verbatim and the server never
looks inside it. A new dashboard has no tiles; add them with
`POST /dashboards/{id}/tiles`.



# Delete a dashboard and every tile on it.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/dashboards/delete-a-dashboard-and-every-tile-on-it

/reference/openapi.json delete /dashboards/{id}
This is the one dashboards route that needs `dashboards:delete`; editing a
dashboard — including adding and removing its tiles — needs only
`dashboards:write`, so a key that can author dashboards cannot necessarily
destroy one. The tiles go with the dashboard; the saved queries they render
are left alone.



# Fetch one dashboard together with its tiles.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/dashboards/fetch-one-dashboard-together-with-its-tiles

/reference/openapi.json get /dashboards/{id}
The response is the dashboard record plus a `tiles` array, ordered by grid
position (top to bottom, then left to right) — the same order the UI draws
them in.



# List a dashboard's tiles, ordered by grid position.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/dashboards/list-a-dashboards-tiles-ordered-by-grid-position

/reference/openapi.json get /dashboards/{id}/tiles
A dashboard id that does not exist in this organization returns an empty
`tiles` array rather than a 404 — check the dashboard itself if you need to
tell "no tiles" from "no dashboard".



# List the organization's dashboards, newest first.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/dashboards/list-the-organizations-dashboards-newest-first

/reference/openapi.json get /dashboards
Dashboards belong to the organization, not to whoever created them —
everyone with `dashboards:read` sees the same list. Each entry carries a
`tile_count` but not the tiles themselves; fetch a single dashboard for
those. The list is cached for up to 30 seconds, so a dashboard created a
moment ago may not appear on the very next call.



# Remove a tile from a dashboard.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/dashboards/remove-a-tile-from-a-dashboard

/reference/openapi.json delete /dashboards/{id}/tiles/{tile_id}
Needs `dashboards:write`, NOT `dashboards:delete` — taking a chart off a
dashboard is an edit; only deleting the whole dashboard needs the delete
grant. The saved query the tile rendered is untouched.



# Replace a dashboard's name, description and definition.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/dashboards/replace-a-dashboards-name-description-and-definition

/reference/openapi.json put /dashboards/{id}
A full replacement, not a patch: send every field you want to keep, because
an omitted `description` is written back as empty. Tiles and their layout
are not touched — change those through the tile endpoints.



# Replace a tile.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/dashboards/replace-a-tile

/reference/openapi.json put /dashboards/{id}/tiles/{tile_id}
A full replacement, not a patch — every field is written, so send the ones
you want to keep. The tile must live on the dashboard named in the path;
otherwise it reads as not found.



# Reposition a dashboard's tiles in one request.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/dashboards/reposition-a-dashboards-tiles-in-one-request

/reference/openapi.json put /dashboards/{id}/tiles/layout
Send `{"tiles": [{id, pos_x, pos_y, pos_w, pos_h}, …]}`; every entry is
applied in a single transaction, so a whole drag-and-resize rearrangement
is one round-trip. Only geometry changes — the query, title and config on
each tile are left as they are.

Positions are validated before anything is written, so a bad entry rejects
the request without applying any of it. But `updated` echoes how many
entries you SENT, not how many rows actually changed: an id that is not a
tile on this dashboard is silently skipped. Send only ids you read back
from the dashboard.



# Enqueue a fresh evaluation job for a session. Used by the dashboard's
re-evaluate button when a session was missed by the automatic pipeline
(e.g. no agent_end ever arrived) or when the user wants fresh scores
after deploying a new evaluator.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/evaluations/enqueue-a-fresh-evaluation-job-for-a-session-used-by-the-dashboardsre-evaluate-button-when-a-session-was-missed-by-the-automatic-pipelineeg-no-agent_end-ever-arrived-or-when-the-user-wants-fresh-scoresafter-deploying-a-new-evaluator

/reference/openapi.json post /sessions/{session_id}/re-evaluate
The `eval_enqueued` guard on `agent_sessions` only gates ingest-driven
enqueue (so duplicate `agent_end` events can't re-evaluate). Manual
re-eval bypasses it: we insert directly into `evaluation_jobs`. The
dispatcher's terminal-result writer already upserts on `session_id`,
so the new run naturally overwrites the previous `evaluations` row.
Re-run the evaluation for one session.

Enqueues a job and returns 202 immediately — the scores are NOT ready when
this returns. Poll `/evaluation-jobs` for progress, `/evaluations` for the
result. The new run overwrites the session's previous evaluation.

Requires `evaluations:trigger`, not `evaluations:read` — a read-only key
cannot start work.

One job per session at a time: if an evaluation for this session is already
queued or in flight, this is a 409. Wait for it to finish, then trigger again.



# List completed evaluations, newest first.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/evaluations/list-completed-evaluations-newest-first

/reference/openapi.json get /evaluations
Cursor-paginated: read a page, then pass its `next_cursor` back as `cursor`.
`next_cursor` is null on the final page. Every filter below AND-composes.

`latest_per_session=true` collapses the page to one row per session — that
session's most recent evaluation — which is what the sessions list shows.
Without it you get the full evaluation history, so a re-evaluated session
appears more than once.



# List the evaluations that are queued or in flight, newest enqueue first.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/evaluations/list-the-evaluations-that-are-queued-or-in-flight-newest-enqueue-first

/reference/openapi.json get /evaluation-jobs
This is the queue, not the results — a job leaves this list once it finishes,
at which point its scores appear on `/evaluations`. Each row carries the
attempt count, the next retry time, and the last error, so a session stuck
behind a failing evaluator is visible here rather than merely absent from
`/evaluations`.



# Rolled-up evaluation health for a filtered slice.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/evaluations/rolled-up-evaluation-health-for-a-filtered-slice

/reference/openapi.json get /evaluations/aggregate
Takes the same filters as `/evaluations` and returns totals, a status
breakdown, per-score-key stats, and a time-bucketed timeline — computed over
the whole matching set, not a sample of it.

`bucket` is a request, not a guarantee: a fine bucket over a long range is
stepped up until the timeline fits 1500 points, and `timeline.bucket_unit`
reports the granularity actually used. `series` is opt-in and capped at 24
series; when the cap bites, `series_truncated` comes back true rather than
the response quietly containing fewer lines than you asked for.



# The distinct environment names seen in this organization's evaluations.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/evaluations/the-distinct-environment-names-seen-in-this-organizations-evaluations

/reference/openapi.json get /evaluations/environments
Returns a bare JSON array of strings, suitable for an environment filter.
Read from the evaluations dataset rather than the event store, so a key with
`evaluations:read` but not `events:read` can still populate the filter.
Cached per organization for 60 seconds, so a brand-new environment can take
up to a minute to show up here.



# The magnitude-metric names under `scores.metrics`, each with its unit.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/evaluations/the-magnitude-metric-names-under-`scoresmetrics`-each-with-its-unit

/reference/openapi.json get /evaluations/metric_keys
Returns a JSON array of `{name, unit, count}` objects. Kept separate from
`score_keys` because the two are on different scales: score keys are 0-1
rates that share one axis, metrics carry units (ms, USD, tokens) and must not
be plotted against each other. `unit` is an empty string for metrics recorded
before units existed. Cached per organization for 60 seconds.

Note the underscore: the path is `/evaluations/metric_keys`.



# The numeric score keys present across this organization's evaluations.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/evaluations/the-numeric-score-keys-present-across-this-organizations-evaluations

/reference/openapi.json get /evaluations/score_keys
Returns a bare JSON array of strings. Score keys are emergent — whatever your
evaluators emit — so this is the complete all-time catalog rather than a
sample of recent rows. Only NUMERIC keys are listed, which is exactly the set
`score_filters` can range-filter on; string and boolean score values are
omitted. Cached per organization for 60 seconds.

Note the underscore: the path is `/evaluations/score_keys`.



# Ingest a batch of events.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/events/ingest-a-batch-of-events

/reference/openapi.json post /events
The body is newline-delimited JSON — one event object per line, not a JSON
array. Malformed lines are SKIPPED, not rejected: the response reports
`accepted` and `skipped` counts and the status is 200 even when every line
was bad. A 5xx means "retry the whole batch"; duplicate events are collapsed
server-side, so retrying is safe.



# List events WITHOUT their payloads — the light feed the dashboard tails.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/events/list-events-without-their-payloads-—-the-light-feed-the-dashboard-tails

/reference/openapi.json get /events/summary
Same filters and cursor semantics as `/events`; each row carries a derived
one-line summary instead of the full payload, so a page is far smaller.



# List raw events, including each event's full payload.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/events/list-raw-events-including-each-events-full-payload

/reference/openapi.json get /events
Cursor-paginated: read a page, then pass its `next_cursor` back as `cursor`.
`next_cursor` is null on the final page. For the dashboard's lighter feed
without payloads, use `/events/summary`.



# List the agent ids this organization has sent events for, most-used first.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/events/list-the-agent-ids-this-organization-has-sent-events-for-most-used-first

/reference/openapi.json get /events/agent_ids
A JSON array of strings — the values accepted by the `agent_id` filter on
`/events`, `/events/summary` and `/sessions`. Capped at the 500 busiest agent
ids and cached for up to a minute.

Either `events:read` or `evaluations:read` grants this, so session-only keys
can populate the same filter.



# List the environment names this organization has actually sent events from.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/events/list-the-environment-names-this-organization-has-actually-sent-events-from

/reference/openapi.json get /events/environments
A JSON array of strings, alphabetically sorted — the values accepted by the
`environment` filter on `/events`, `/events/summary` and `/sessions`. Derived
from stored events, so an environment appears only once something has been
ingested under it, and results are cached for up to a minute: a brand-new
environment can take that long to show up.

Either `events:read` or `evaluations:read` grants this, so session-only keys
can populate the same filter.



# List the error types seen in this organization's events, most-used first.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/events/list-the-error-types-seen-in-this-organizations-events-most-used-first

/reference/openapi.json get /events/error_types
A JSON array of strings — the values accepted by the `error_type` filter.
Only events that carry a classified error type are counted, which is a
narrower set than `errored=true`: a failed tool result that reports an error
message without a type contributes to that filter but not to this list.
Capped at 500 values, cached for a couple of minutes.



# List the event types this organization has actually sent, alphabetically.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/events/list-the-event-types-this-organization-has-actually-sent-alphabetically

/reference/openapi.json get /events/event_types
A JSON array of strings — the values accepted by the `event_type` filter.
This is the observed set, not the full catalogue the SDKs can emit: a type
you have never ingested is absent. Cached for up to five minutes, the longest
of the facet endpoints.



# List the hook names seen in this organization's events, most-used first.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/events/list-the-hook-names-seen-in-this-organizations-events-most-used-first

/reference/openapi.json get /events/hook_names
A JSON array of strings — the values accepted by the `hook_name` filter.
Counted from `hook_triggered` events only (the start leg of a hook), capped
at 500 names, cached for a couple of minutes.



# List the model names seen in this organization's events, most-used first.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/events/list-the-model-names-seen-in-this-organizations-events-most-used-first

/reference/openapi.json get /events/models
A JSON array of strings — the values accepted by the `model` filter. Capped
at the 500 most-used models and cached for up to a minute. Every event that
names a model contributes, not just model responses, so both legs of a model
call count towards the ordering.



# List the tool names seen in this organization's events, most-used first.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/events/list-the-tool-names-seen-in-this-organizations-events-most-used-first

/reference/openapi.json get /events/tool_names
A JSON array of strings — the values accepted by the `tool_name` filter.
Counted from `tool_use` and `tool_result` events only, capped at 500 names,
cached for a couple of minutes.



# List the trigger events that fired hooks recently, most-used first.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/events/list-the-trigger-events-that-fired-hooks-recently-most-used-first

/reference/openapi.json get /events/trigger_events
A JSON array of strings — the values accepted by the `trigger_event` filter.
Only the last 90 days are scanned, so a trigger that has not fired in that
window is absent even though older events still carry it. Capped at 500
values and cached for up to a minute.



# Roll up the latency between two event types into a chart-ready summary.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/events/roll-up-the-latency-between-two-event-types-into-a-chart-ready-summary

/reference/openapi.json get /events/latency_aggregate
Pairs each `start_event_type` event with its matching `end_event_type` event
and reports the duration between them: `bins` (a time series over the
window), `heatmap` (time against latency band), `summary` (pair count with
p50/p95/p99 and max), `events` (window totals), and, when
`distribution_key_paths` is given, a `distribution` broken down by that key.
This is how the tools, models and hooks pages are drawn.

`start_event_type` and `end_event_type` are required and must differ;
anything else returns 400. `ts_to` defaults to now, and omitting `ts_from`
spans back to the oldest matching event rather than a fixed window — check
`bounds` in the response for what was actually covered. `bin_count` defaults
to 24 and is clamped to 1–168. The distribution names the top 10 keys and
rolls the rest into a single `(other)` entry, so it still sums to the window
total.

Two behaviours worth knowing. `payload_sum_paths` can only sum `duration_ms`,
`input_tokens` and `output_tokens` — any other path is ignored silently and
its `sums` entry stays 0. And sums count only the closing event of each pair,
so token usage reported on both legs is not double-counted.



# Summarise the errors matching a filter, across the whole window.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/events/summarise-the-errors-matching-a-filter-across-the-whole-window

/reference/openapi.json get /events/error_summary
Returns `total`, the number of distinct `sessions` and `agents` involved,
`last_ts` (null when nothing matched), a `bins` array of exactly 24 counts,
and the `bounds` in epoch milliseconds that those bins span.

Two things to know. The result is ALWAYS restricted to errored events, so it
is not a general event rollup — the same filters here and on
`/events/summary?errored=true` describe the same set, which is what keeps a
chart and its rows in agreement. And when `ts_from`/`ts_to` are omitted, the
bins span the matched data's own first and last event rather than a fixed
window, so `bounds` is the only reliable way to turn a bin index back into a
time range. Counts are computed over the entire window, not the current page,
and are cached for about ten seconds.



# Liveness probe.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/health/liveness-probe

/reference/openapi.json get /health
The only endpoint on `/v1` that needs no credential — it reports that the
process is answering, nothing about your data.



# Acknowledge an issue — "I'm looking at this".
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/issues/acknowledge-an-issue-—-"im-looking-at-this"

/reference/openapi.json post /issues/{iid}/ack
Needs only `issues:read`, deliberately: signalling that you have picked
something up must not require write authority. It does not change who is
accountable — `POST /issues/{iid}/assign` does that.

More than one person may ack, and each one lands an attributed row on the
activity log, but `acknowledged_at` / `acknowledged_by` keep recording the
FIRST ack, so a retry or a double-click cannot inflate time-to-acknowledge.
Acking also subscribes you to the thread.



# Comment on an issue.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/issues/comment-on-an-issue

/reference/openapi.json post /issues/{iid}/comments
`body` is required and capped at 8000 characters after trimming. Needs only
`issues:read`: a responder who can see the issue can talk on its thread —
putting discussion behind a write grant would make read-only reviewers silent
observers. Commenting subscribes you to the thread and emails the other
subscribers.



# Count issues without fetching them.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/issues/count-issues-without-fetching-them

/reference/openapi.json get /issues/count
Returns `{ "count": n }` for the same `state` filter `GET /issues` takes
(default `firing,acknowledged`). This is what the sidebar badge polls, so a
dashboard does not pull 200 rows to render one number. Cached for 15 seconds,
so it can trail a state change by that long.



# Delete a comment.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/issues/delete-a-comment

/reference/openapi.json delete /issues/{iid}/comments/{cid}
Authorship, not permission tier, is the gate: you may delete your own
comment, and holders of `issues:close` may moderate anyone's — someone has to
be able to remove a departed colleague's. A bare API-key call carries no
human identity and so cannot prove authorship; it needs `issues:close`.

The delete is soft. The comment stays in the thread as a tombstone with
`body: null` rather than vanishing. Returns 204 with no body.



# Fetch one issue, with its whole thread.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/issues/fetch-one-issue-with-its-whole-thread

/reference/openapi.json get /issues/{iid}
Beyond the issue's own fields this returns `notifications` (the last 100
delivery attempts, newest first, each with its channel and status),
`subscribers`, `comments` (oldest first — deleted ones appear as tombstones
with `body: null`) and `activity`, the append-only log of who did what. An
issue that graduated from an audit finding also carries `finding`, a snapshot
of that finding refreshed on every audit run; other issues omit the field
entirely. Cached for 30 seconds.



# List an issue's comments.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/issues/list-an-issues-comments

/reference/openapi.json get /issues/{iid}/comments
Oldest first. Deleted comments are still returned, as tombstones with
`body: null`, so the thread keeps its shape and reply order.



# List issues.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/issues/list-issues

/reference/openapi.json get /issues
The whole issues board in one feed: issues opened by an alert rule, issues
graduated from an audit finding, and issues opened by hand. Newest first.

`state` defaults to `firing,acknowledged`, so resolved issues are hidden
until you ask for them. Unrecognised states are dropped rather than
rejected — `?state=closed` returns `[]`, not an error. `limit` defaults to
200 and is capped at 1000; there is no cursor, so narrow with `state` or
`alert_id` instead of paging. Cached for 10 seconds.



# List who gets an issue's activity emails.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/issues/list-who-gets-an-issues-activity-emails

/reference/openapi.json get /issues/{iid}/subscribers
Active subscribers only — anyone who unsubscribed is omitted. Note that
people are subscribed automatically when they ack, comment, are assigned, or
open the issue, so this is not just the list of manual subscribes.



# Open an issue by hand, with no parent alert.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/issues/open-an-issue-by-hand-with-no-parent-alert

/reference/openapi.json post /issues
For a failure that doesn't map to any configured rule. `summary` is required
and capped at 2000 characters; `title` is optional and falls back to the
summary's first 200 characters; `severity` is `info`, `warning` (the default)
or `critical`.

An issue opened this way never fans out through alert channels — there is no
parent whose channels it could inherit — so it is a triage thread and
nothing more. You are subscribed to it automatically.



# Replace an issue's assignees.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/issues/replace-an-issues-assignees

/reference/openapi.json post /issues/{iid}/assign
A whole-list replace, not an add: `{"assignees": []}` clears everyone. (The
older single `assigned_to` string is still accepted — a string becomes a
one-element list, `null` clears — and is ignored when `assignees` is
present.) Every address must belong to an active member of your
organization; a typo or an outsider is rejected 422 before anything is
written, so the call never half-applies.

The permission check is on the DIFF, not on the request. With `issues:read`
you may take YOURSELF off the list, or send a no-op; adding anybody, or
removing somebody else, needs `issues:create` and is otherwise 403. Everyone
left on the list, plus you, is subscribed to the thread.



# Resolve an issue.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/issues/resolve-an-issue

/reference/openapi.json post /issues/{iid}/resolve
The one triage action with its own permission — `issues:close`, not the
`issues:read` the rest of the thread runs on — because closing is what
silences the thread and takes the issue off the board.

For an issue that graduated from an audit finding, the finding is resolved in
the SAME transaction, so a later audit run cannot quietly reopen it.
Resolving an already-resolved issue is a 409, not a no-op.



# Stop an issue's activity emails.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/issues/stop-an-issues-activity-emails

/reference/openapi.json post /issues/{iid}/unsubscribe
The mirror of subscribe. Removing YOURSELF — the default with no body — works
at `issues:read`, so nobody can be trapped on a thread; passing another
person's `email` takes them off it and needs `issues:create`.



# Subscribe to an issue's activity emails.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/issues/subscribe-to-an-issues-activity-emails

/reference/openapi.json post /issues/{iid}/subscribe
With no body you subscribe yourself, using the email your dashboard session
forwards. Passing `{"email": …}` for SOMEONE ELSE is a create-tier action: it
needs `issues:create`, and that address must belong to an active member of
your organization. Subscribing yourself works at `issues:read`, so a
read-only responder who acked can always manage their own notifications.

Idempotent — re-subscribing clears any earlier unsubscribe.



# List this organization's API keys.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/keys/list-this-organizations-api-keys

/reference/openapi.json get /keys
Secrets are never returned — only metadata. A key's secret is shown once, at
creation, and cannot be recovered afterwards.



# Mint a scoped API key.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/keys/mint-a-scoped-api-key

/reference/openapi.json post /keys
You supply the secret in `key`; the server stores only its hash and never
returns it again. Generate it with a cryptographically secure random source.
`permissions` defaults to `["events:add"]` — an ingest-only key.



# Replace a key's permissions.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/keys/replace-a-keys-permissions

/reference/openapi.json patch /keys/{id}
No API key can call this. `keys:update` is deliberately not grantable to any
key — editing keys is a human, dashboard-only action — so a bearer token
always gets 403 here, permanently and by design. Use the dashboard's key
editor instead. The list you send replaces the key's grants outright rather
than adding to them, and keys seeded from configuration cannot be edited.



# Revoke an API key.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/keys/revoke-an-api-key

/reference/openapi.json post /keys/{id}/disable
Revocation is permanent — there is no re-enable, so mint a replacement rather
than expecting to undo this. It takes effect immediately on the replica
handling the request and within 5 seconds on every other replica. Keys seeded
from configuration (the bootstrap admin, the dashboard assistant) are
protected and cannot be revoked over the API.



# Rotate a key's secret.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/keys/rotate-a-keys-secret

/reference/openapi.json post /keys/{id}/regenerate
The server generates the new secret and returns it in `key`; this is the only
time it is shown. The old secret stops working immediately on this replica and
within 5 seconds elsewhere, so anything still using it starts failing as soon
as you rotate. The key's id, name and permissions are unchanged. Revoked keys
cannot be rotated, and keys seeded from configuration are protected.



# Define a new permission set.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/permission-sets/define-a-new-permission-set

/reference/openapi.json post /permission-sets
`permissions` is the list of grants the set confers; every entry must be a
known permission and the list may not repeat one. Names are trimmed, capped
at 64 characters, and unique within the organization. The set is created
with no members — assign it to users through `/users`.

Note the asymmetry: writing a set needs `settings:write`, while reading one
needs `users:read`.



# Delete a permission set.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/permission-sets/delete-a-permission-set

/reference/openapi.json delete /permission-sets/{name}
Members assigned to it keep the permissions they already have — they simply
stop being linked to a set — and the response reports how many were
unlinked as `affected_users`.

Two sets refuse deletion with 409: a builtin, and whichever set is currently
named by this organization's `default_user_permissions` setting. Point that
setting at another set before deleting this one.

Note the asymmetry: writing a set needs `settings:write`, while reading one
needs `users:read`.



# One permission set, with its grants.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/permission-sets/one-permission-set-with-its-grants

/reference/openapi.json get /permission-sets/{name}
Reuses the list's gate (`users:read`) for the same reason: the create-user
form needs it and reading a set exposes nothing beyond its name and grants.
Writing one, by contrast, needs `settings:write`.



# Replace a permission set's grants and description.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/permission-sets/replace-a-permission-sets-grants-and-description

/reference/openapi.json put /permission-sets/{name}
`permissions` is the complete new list, not a delta — anything you omit is
removed. Every member of this organization assigned to the set has their
effective permissions re-materialised as part of the request, so the change
takes effect on those users' next call rather than after a cache expiry.

Builtin sets (`read-only`, `standard`, `admin`) are immutable and refuse the
write with 409, so those names always mean the same thing.

Note the asymmetry: writing a set needs `settings:write`, while reading one
needs `users:read`.



# The permission sets defined for your organization.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/permission-sets/the-permission-sets-defined-for-your-organization

/reference/openapi.json get /permission-sets
Each entry carries its grants and a `user_count` of the enabled members
currently assigned to it, so a UI can show "applied to N users". Builtins
(`read-only`, `standard`, `admin`) sort first and are marked `is_builtin`.

Reading a set needs `users:read`, NOT `settings:read` — the create-user form
is open to anyone with `users:create` and has to populate its picker, and
listing carries no privilege beyond seeing names. Creating or changing a set
is the asymmetric half: that needs `settings:write`.



# Delete a saved query.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/queries/delete-a-saved-query

/reference/openapi.json delete /queries/{id}
Needs `queries:delete`, a separate grant from the `queries:write` used to
author one. Refused with 409 while any dashboard tile still renders it —
remove those tiles first.



# Describe the tables a query may read.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/queries/describe-the-tables-a-query-may-read

/reference/openapi.json get /queries/schema
Returns `{schema, tables: [{name, columns: [{name, type}]}]}` — the same
listing the query editor's autocomplete and schema browser are built on.
Types are normalised display names (`string`, `int`, `float`, `timestamp`,
`uuid`, `bool`), with a trailing `?` when the column is nullable.

The shape is the same for every organization; only the rows a query over
these tables returns are yours.



# Fetch one saved query, including its SQL.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/queries/fetch-one-saved-query-including-its-sql

/reference/openapi.json get /queries/{id}



# List the organization's saved queries, alphabetically by name.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/queries/list-the-organizations-saved-queries-alphabetically-by-name

/reference/openapi.json get /queries
Saved queries belong to the organization, not to whoever wrote them. Each
entry includes its full `sql_text` and declared `params`. The list is cached
for up to 30 seconds, so a query saved a moment ago may not appear on the
very next call.



# Replace a saved query's name, description, SQL and params.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/queries/replace-a-saved-querys-name-description-sql-and-params

/reference/openapi.json put /queries/{id}
A full replacement, not a patch: send every field you want to keep, because
an omitted `description` is written back as empty. Dashboard tiles that
render this query pick up the new SQL the next time they are run — editing
a query changes every chart built on it.



# Run SQL and get rows back.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/queries/run-sql-and-get-rows-back

/reference/openapi.json post /queries/run
Send either `sql` (free-form) or `query_id` (a saved query to execute); if
both are present `sql` wins and `query_id` is recorded only as the run's
origin. `params` is a JSON array of positional values substituted for
`$1`…`$N` in the statement.

Results are scoped to your organization no matter how the SQL is written —
there is no way to phrase a query that reads another organization's data.

One read-only statement is accepted and nothing else:

* it must start with `SELECT` or `WITH`;
* a `;` outside a string literal is rejected — no multi-statement bodies;
* 8000 characters maximum;
* a single statement may not join the analytics tables (`events`,
  `evaluations`, `agent_sessions`) to the operational ones (`dashboards`,
  `saved_queries`, `api_keys`, `users`, …) — split it into two queries.

Use `GET /queries/schema` for the tables and columns you can read.

A successful run returns `{columns, rows, truncated, elapsed_ms}`, where
each entry in `rows` is an array of values positionally matching `columns`.
At most 10 000 rows come back; `truncated` is `true` when there were more,
so page with `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` in your own SQL rather than relying on the
cap. A run is cut off after 10 seconds.

A `NUMERIC` column comes back as `null` — cast it in the SELECT
(`avg(x)::float8`).

Every run, including a rejected or failed one, is recorded in the query
audit log with its SQL, parameters, duration and outcome.



# Save a query.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/queries/save-a-query

/reference/openapi.json post /queries
`sql_text` is stored exactly as written and is NOT checked here — the
restrictions on what may run are applied at execution time, so SQL that
saves cleanly can still be refused by `POST /queries/run`. Names must be
unique within the organization.

`params` is a JSON array declaring the query's positional parameters for the
editor; the server stores it verbatim and never interprets it.



# Download one session's full event log as a file.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/sessions/download-one-sessions-full-event-log-as-a-file

/reference/openapi.json get /sessions/{session_id}/export
The response is a single JSON object — session metadata plus every event in
the session, oldest first, each with its full payload — served as an
attachment (`Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="session-<id>.json"`).
These are the exact bytes an evaluator receives for the session, so a
downloaded file can be replayed through an evaluator unchanged.

There is no pagination and no size cap: a long session downloads in full, in
one response. `session_id` is scoped to your organization — a session
belonging to another organization reads as unknown and returns 404.



# List agent sessions with their latest evaluation headline.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/sessions/list-agent-sessions-with-their-latest-evaluation-headline

/reference/openapi.json get /sessions
Requires `evaluations:read` rather than `events:read` — the row a session
returns is its evaluation summary, not its events.



# Change one setting for your organization.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/settings/change-one-setting-for-your-organization

/reference/openapi.json put /settings/{key}
Send either `{"value": ...}` or the bare value — both are accepted. The
value is validated against the setting's schema before it is stored, and the
updated row is returned. The change applies only to your organization.

Two keys carry an extra check and reject with 422:
`default_user_permissions` must name a permission set that exists in this
org, and `allowed_sign_ins` may not be saved as a list that excludes the
operator making the change — that list filters who may sign in, and the
settings page is behind that sign-in, so there would be no way back in.



# Every registered setting, with your organization's current value.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/settings/every-registered-setting-with-your-organizations-current-value

/reference/openapi.json get /settings
Settings are per-organization: each entry is this org's stored value, or the
registry default for a key the org has never set. Every entry carries the
setting's `schema`, so a UI can render a typed input without re-declaring the
catalogue. Secrets never leave the server in the clear — their `value` comes
back empty and a `value_set` flag says whether one is stored.



# Preview the context window a model resolves to.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/settings/preview-the-context-window-a-model-resolves-to

/reference/openapi.json get /settings/model-context-windows/resolve
Returns the effective limit and its authoritative `source`: `override` (this
org configured it), `default` (AgentEye's built-in table), or `unknown` (no
limit known, so no context-fill percentage is computed). Deliberately does
not consult the cache, so it reports the true source rather than a cache hit.

The model id travels in the `model` QUERY parameter, not the path, so ids
containing `/` need no percent-encoding.



# Remove one model's context-window override.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/settings/remove-one-models-context-window-override

/reference/openapi.json delete /settings/model-context-windows
The model falls back to AgentEye's built-in default from the next ingested
event. 404 if this organization has no override for that model.

The model id travels in the `model` QUERY parameter, not the path, so ids
containing `/` need no percent-encoding.



# Set the context window for one model, for your organization.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/settings/set-the-context-window-for-one-model-for-your-organization

/reference/openapi.json put /settings/model-context-windows
Body: `{ "model_id": "...", "context_window": N }`. Creates the override or
replaces the one already stored for that model id. `context_window` is in
tokens and must be between 0 and 1000000; 0 means "unknown", so no
context-fill percentage is computed for that model. The new value applies
from the next ingested event.

The model id travels in the BODY, not the path — which is why ids containing
`/` need no percent-encoding, and why this shares its path with the list and
delete operations.



# The context-window overrides configured for your organization.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/settings/the-context-window-overrides-configured-for-your-organization

/reference/openapi.json get /settings/model-context-windows
One entry per model id this org has overridden; models left on AgentEye's
built-in defaults do not appear here. To see what a specific model actually
resolves to, override or not, use `/settings/model-context-windows/resolve`.

Listing, setting and deleting all share this one path and differ only by
method, because the model id travels in the body or the query string rather
than the path.



# The setting catalogue — key, type, and constraints, with no values.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/settings/the-setting-catalogue-—-key-type-and-constraints-with-no-values

/reference/openapi.json get /settings/schema
Registry metadata only, so it reads nothing per-organization and returns the
same document for every caller. Use it to render typed inputs without
re-declaring the catalogue; use `GET /settings` when you also need values.



# Historical billing windows, most recent first.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/usage/historical-billing-windows-most-recent-first

/reference/openapi.json get /usage/windows
One entry per completed window plus the one in progress, so a caller can
chart usage over time without knowing the organization's billing anchor.



# Usage totals for the organization's current billing window.
Source: https://docs.befailproof.ai/api-reference/usage/usage-totals-for-the-organizations-current-billing-window

/reference/openapi.json get /usage
Defaults to the window containing now; pass `window_start` to read a
specific one. Window boundaries follow the organization's own billing
anchor, so they are not calendar months.
